``` Coming up with a formal proof that is completely correct and accepted by the scientific community is not easy. Writing a proof is a very difficult and time-consuming task and later checking the correctness of it requires a lot of time. Writing a proof typically involves a lot of mathematical deduction (aka reasoning), each proof step having a logically sound sequence of reasoning arriving at the next step. Complex proofs use reasoning from multiple sources. An AI can speed up the proof writing, verification, or both. An AI can help humans in a form of human-AI collaboration. It may suggest/reason a sequence of deduction(s) or the way to approach actual writing and verification.

It is possible for an AI to write proofs based on its internal training and reasoning. Such approaches often involve splitting the proof into multiple different proof parts and attempt to solve them one by one. This approach typically is useful for problems with attemptable subproblems.

For example, AI recently resolved the Erdős used to have ($\bar{g}(k)$) for small values of $k$.

Another approach is based on the existing proofs. Even if the goal is to prove something that was not yet proved, if the existence of similar theories, formulations, or proofs exist, an AI may be able to use it as a starting point and apply similar arguments to the new problem. If precise analogs do not yet exist, a human may still look for inspiration. An AI may try to relate the new problem to known patterns or the existing proofs and come up with its own conclusions.

The last approach is based on the generative AI. A common AI approach is to attempt substitute the inductive step of the proof-of-concept by computing each step using the generative capabilities of an AI system. AI-based proof validation may be attempted both by using correct logic and by using AI-based natural language understanding.

Even after the proof of a large conjecture is found, there is a course-adjacent reliance on AI systems to recreate the correctness of it in terms of a recognized formal logical framework.

Here are two examples of alleged completed systems. Namely, "Automated Verification of Ramanujan’s Logarithmic Integrals by Deep Neural Networks" and "Towards Certifiable Input-Adaptive Factuality in LLMs: Verification Ability and Accuracy in AI Proof Assistants".
Given the results of these attempts, it appears a standard consensus of correctness approach would not be able to certify the actual correctness of these proofs. It would require some form of a formal logical framework to prove these two papers themselves, which would most likely recur with different formal frameworks.

Human voice reciprocity can also create a challenge. Humans have a tendency to either give credit to the AI for a pure idea or have a tendency to (wrongfully) downplay the contributions given by an AI. These human behaviors would be not helpful in effectively highlighting AI's capability gaps or any formal logical framework-based assertions of correctness.

Avoiding future human-AI collaboration bias. To avoid any type of future current human-AI collaboration challenges, it will be necessary for the scientific community to agree on a mechanism to measure and allow for effective bias corrections.

Personal opinion: The AI intended to solve these problems is not clear at the time of writing this forecasting. The AI community is growing rapidly, many humans are peaking at their capabilities. Any given AI may only be successful at the tasks that it is specialized towards which may not be conducive to solving this types of problems.
